paragraphs: In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers.

The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business.

Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms.

The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.

Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration.

Cantor Fitzgerald has had business dealings with several data center companies in Southeast Asia that cater to Chinese clients, and could be affected by the regulations Mr. Lutnick is drafting, a review by The New York Times has found.

Cantor Fitzgerald served as a designated sales agent for an equity offering of up to $1 billion this year by Bitdeer, the Singaporean firm that will operate data center A201, in addition to having other financial ties to various global data center businesses. The relationship between the two companies began as early as 2024, when Cantor Fitzgerald helped Bitdeer arrange a stock offering of up to $250 million.

Mr. Lutnick steered Cantor Fitzgerald for decades, before recusing himself when he joined the Trump administration last year. The Commerce Department says Mr. Lutnick has complied with all ethics agreements, and his former business is now run by his sons.

These dealings are just a tiny portion of Cantor’s business, which stretches from investment banking and trading to real estate. Other investment banks have similar partnerships, and there is no evidence that Cantor’s investments influenced Mr. Lutnick’s deliberations.

But the overlapping relationships are the latest indication of the potential conflicts that exist given Mr. Lutnick’s role in shaping rules around U.S. technology exports. And they demonstrate how the U.S. ban on selling chips directly to China has led to an explosion of data centers in Southeast Asia aimed at Chinese customers. It is now up to Mr. Lutnick to decide whether to tighten the rules in ways that would cut off this avenue.
In the administration, Mr. Lutnick has been seen as one of Nvidia’s strongest champions.
His department has been increasingly criticized in recent months for giving Nvidia unusual access to rule-making and investigations, and standing in the way of sanctions on Nvidia’s customers.

The issue has been thrust into the spotlight in recent weeks with the scandal over the Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman the U.S. government deemed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

The woman, Alice Huang, had led Megaspeed, a firm that set up data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese companies. The U.S. government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling chips into China.
The United States in late 2022 started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons.
But while Chinese firms cannot buy Nvidia’s most advanced chips outright, nothing stops them from renting those chips in data centers in Malaysia, Indonesia or Thailand.

The arrangement is viewed by many in Washington as a harmful loophole. While some argue that the sales help U.S. leadership in technology, many in the administration have argued for clamping down, and Congress is considering a bipartisan bill to do so.

In its final weeks, the Biden administration issued global rules to restrict the ability of Chinese companies to remotely access U.S. chips. But President Trump revoked those rules when he came into office, arguing that they stifled American business and innovation.
Trump officials said they would introduce a new rule to replace the Biden ones. But they have struggled to reconcile competing views in the administration about how aggressive the rules should be.

Mr. Lutnick has been described as delaying or deferring these technology controls at several points in the past year, arguing that they could affect companies like Nvidia, or U.S. trade relations with China and other countries.

People familiar with the discussions say the Commerce Department has pushed for a more scaled-back version of the rule. The department has proposed applying regulations to a handful of countries — Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, South Africa and Norway. Others in the administration have wanted global coverage.
The proposal was first reported by The Information.

The Commerce Department proposal would also apply only to future shipments of advanced chips, exempting data centers already filled with American technology. Companies would need to notify the government if Chinese customers use their data centers to train A.I. models. But they would not automatically need to obtain a license.
The Commerce Department had also argued for the rules to kick in when companies are using a larger amount of computing power, meaning fewer activities by Chinese companies would be regulated.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official, predicted that Chinese companies would find ways to sidestep the more narrow controls the Commerce Department is proposing.
“If you’re only restricting remote access to data centers in certain countries, then China will just rent from the data centers outside those countries,” he said.

Nvidia had been one of Cantor’s largest stock positions early last year, but last fall, the firm began steadily selling off shares. Cantor holds those shares on behalf of clients, not as part of its proprietary investment portfolio.
Still, Cantor Fitzgerald continued to help arrange billions of dollars of financing for industries ranging from data centers to cryptocurrency that depend on a steady supply of computing from Nvidia.
That includes Bitdeer, which is building out the Malaysian data center it expects to generate $1.7 billion in revenue over five years, according to a company statement.

That data center will likely serve Tencent, a Chinese internet giant that would be able to gain access to Nvidia’s most advanced A.I. servers, according to a person with knowledge of the arrangement. Bitdeer is part of Nvidia’s partner network, a program for companies that work closely with the chipmaker.

Bitdeer hosts a Chinese language website that lets customers rent A.I. chips and gain access to Chinese open source A.I. models through data centers in Malaysia, Canada and elsewhere. The Johor facility is one of five data centers the company plans to open in Malaysia in the coming years, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Cantor holds a stake in Bitdeer through its investment in Tether, the crypto company. It is far from the only American financial heavyweight investing in overseas data centers. Bain Capital, Citadel and Blackstone have all poured money into A.I. computing clusters across the region.

Cantor also previously provided financial services to Gorilla Technology, which is building data centers in Thailand and Indonesia, and has a contract to provide A.I. computing to Freyr AI, a Singaporean data center firm that corporate filings and job ads indicate has ties to China.
Cantor has worked with other Nvidia partners globally, including IREN, an Australian cloud computing company, and Lancium, a Texas data center developer.

A Commerce Department spokeswoman said that Mr. Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the United States. He does not discuss department matters with his sons, nor do they discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him, she added.
Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment. Bitdeer did not reply to a request for comment.

Mr. Lutnick, as of October 2025, transferred his remaining ownership stake in Cantor to his family. Before that, he had been given what the White House had called a “limited waiver” that allowed him to participate in certain decisions that could have “a direct and predictable effect on Cantor Fitzgerald,” exempting him from a federal criminal law that would otherwise have required him to entirely recuse himself from these discussions.

Even after Mr. Lutnick finished transferring his ownership stake to his sons late last year, he still had to abide by an ethics rule prohibiting federal employees from using their public office for their private gain or the gain of friends and relatives.

The Times reported last year that Mr. Lutnick was promoting data center projects that worked with his family firms. Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, and two dozen other Democratic lawmakers called for an investigation.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official, predicted that Chinese companies would find ways to sidestep the more narrow controls the Commerce Department is proposing.

“If you’re only restricting remote access to data centers in certain countries, then China will just rent from the data centers outside those countries,” he said.

Nvidia had been one of Cantor’s largest stock positions early last year, but last fall, the firm began steadily selling off shares. Cantor holds those shares on behalf of clients, not as part of its proprietary investment portfolio.

Still, Cantor Fitzgerald continued to help arrange billions of dollars of financing for industries ranging from data centers to cryptocurrency that depend on a steady supply of computing from Nvidia.

That includes Bitdeer, which is building out the Malaysian data center it expects to generate $1.7 billion in revenue over five years, according to a company statement.

That data center will likely serve Tencent, a Chinese internet giant that would be able to gain access to Nvidia’s most advanced A.I. servers, according to a person with knowledge of the arrangement. Bitdeer is part of Nvidia’s partner network, a program for companies that work closely with the chipmaker.

Bitdeer hosts a Chinese language website that lets customers rent A.I. chips and gain access to Chinese open source A.I. models through data centers in Malaysia, Canada and elsewhere. The Johor facility is one of five data centers the company plans to open in Malaysia in the coming years, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Cantor holds a stake in Bitdeer through its investment in Tether, the crypto company. It is far from the only American financial heavyweight investing in overseas data centers. Bain Capital, Citadel and Blackstone have all poured money into A.I. computing clusters across the region.

Cantor also previously provided financial services to Gorilla Technology, which is building data centers in Thailand and Indonesia, and has a contract to provide A.I. computing to Freyr AI, a Singaporean data center firm that corporate filings and job ads indicate has ties to China.

Cantor has worked with other Nvidia partners globally, including IREN, an Australian cloud computing company, and Lancium, a Texas data center developer.

A Commerce Department spokeswoman said that Mr. Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the United States. He does not discuss department matters with his sons, nor do they discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him, she added.

Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment. Bitdeer did not reply to a request for comment.

Mr. Lutnick, as of October 2025, transferred his remaining ownership stake in Cantor to his family. Before that, he had been given what the White House had called a “limited waiver” that allowed him to participate in certain decisions that could have “a direct and predictable effect on Cantor Fitzgerald,” exempting him from a federal criminal law that would otherwise have required him to entirely recuse himself from these discussions.

Even after Mr. Lutnick finished transferring his ownership stake to his sons late last year, he still had to abide by an ethics rule prohibiting federal employees from using their public office for their private gain or the gain of friends and relatives.

The Times reported last year that Mr. Lutnick was promoting data center projects that worked with his family firms. Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, and two dozen other Democratic lawmakers called for an investigation.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/us/fa.lead_paragraph: The Federal Aviation Administration has suspended its installation of routers like the one that transportation officials said they believed had contributed to a nationwide ground stop on Friday after it overloaded communications systems used by air traffic controllers and pilots.
paragraphs: The Federal Aviation Administration has suspended its installation of routers like the one that transportation officials said they believed had contributed to a nationwide ground stop on Friday after it overloaded communications systems used by air traffic controllers and pilots.

The broadcasting function of more than 60 other identical devices on the network was disabled after the disruptions wreaked havoc on air travel, according to the F.A.A., which said on Tuesday that the changes had taken effect in quick succession in response to the chain of events on Friday.

Made by Juniper Networks, which was acquired last year by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, the routers were intended to replace older Cisco Systems models as part of a sweeping program by the F.A.A. to modernize its equipment.
For decades, copper wiring has been the backbone of that antiquated system, which the federal government has slowly started to replace with modern fiber-optic cables.

But while an engineer was installing one of the replacement routers on Friday at an F.A.A. radio center in El Dorado, Ark., data began flooding the network, overwhelming the system and hampering communications, federal officials said. That engineer was working for L3Harris, the company that owns the network used by the F.A.A., and was being monitored by an F.A.A. technician, officials said.
A second router at an F.A.A. radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, also became unstable, according to the F.A.A., which said technicians had resolved the problem by disabling both routers.
“So we thought it’s only prudent to pause the use of these routers,” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said at a news conference on Tuesday on Capitol Hill.
Mr. Duffy suggested the router glitch was isolated, saying that federal officials had grounded flights out of an abundance of caution.
“Sixty-eight times it worked well,” he said earlier in the news conference. “This one router started to broadcast into our network, and it started to overload the network.”
Federal transportation officials said on Tuesday that the replacement routers had been tested for a year before being installed.
“We don’t know the fault trigger,” Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, said at the news conference. “We do know that this router could be enabled to do what it did.”
In a statement on Tuesday, Adam Bauer, a spokesman for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, disputed that the Juniper Networks device was defective.

“Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured,” Mr. Bauer said. “The F.A.A. is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause.”
On Monday, Democratic members of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee sent a letter to Mr. Duffy and Mr. Bedford urging them to pause the use of the Juniper Networks routers.

“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed,” the senators wrote. “F.A.A. must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.”

On Tuesday, federal officials were less measured in their assessment of the performance of L3Harris, which Mr. Duffy said had held contracts with the F.A.A. for more than 20 years and was responsible for monitoring the network.
“They didn’t identify and isolate,” he said. “That concerns me. We have to have them perform better.”
A representative for L3Harris on Tuesday referred to a previous statement, which said the company was “supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation.”
While Mr. Duffy said there was no evidence that the system had been hacked, he noted that F.B.I. analysts were examining the router from the F.A.A. radio facility in Arkansas.

Mr. Bedford said that air traffic controllers had never lost contact with planes while the network was experiencing disruptions. He added that the F.A.A. had backup systems in place but that safety was paramount.
“And people can fly with confidence,” he said.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/techn.lead_paragraph: In 2023, as the artificial intelligence boom took off, Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were pitching investors in Shanghai on a plan to build an A.I. business in Southeast Asia.
paragraphs: In 2023, as the artificial intelligence boom took off, Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were pitching investors in Shanghai on a plan to build an A.I. business in Southeast Asia.

Working from a colonial mansion in the city’s former French Concession neighborhood, the couple boasted about Ms. Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, who they said would guarantee a supply of powerful computer chips.

They also hinted at a deep-pocketed customer that would pay for access to those chips and anchor the business, according to two people who attended the meetings. The company created after those pitch sessions, a Singapore firm called Megaspeed, purchased more than $4 billion in Nvidia chips over the next few years.

Megaspeed’s customer and financial backer turned out to be Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant, according to three people familiar with the relationship. Alibaba is a colossus, with a wide range of businesses. It also co-founded an A.I. lab with strong ties to China’s military, where researchers have worked on tasks such as automating cyberattacks and simulating war games.

For the past several weeks, Nvidia has been convulsed by revelations that Mr. Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence and was passing information to Beijing. But beneath the scandal is a geopolitical tug of war over access to the advanced Nvidia chips that help power the global A.I. boom.

The web of relationships between Megaspeed, Alibaba and Nvidia exposes a supply chain that often circumvents efforts by the United States to keep those chips out of China’s reach. The fact that Alibaba has access to the Nvidia chips and is only one step removed from the military-linked A.I. lab is exactly what intelligence officials in Washington have long feared. The technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.
The facility, called Zhejiang Lab, has another important link to Nvidia. Its current director, Wang Jian, was Alibaba’s chief technology officer and has had a long friendship with Nvidia’s Mr. Huang.

Whether Nvidia chips supplied by Megaspeed went from Alibaba to the lab is unclear. But the ties show how advanced computing reaches sensitive Chinese institutions through layers of contractors and resellers that obscure the origin of the chips. It also underscores how closely Alibaba, the company that anchored Ms. Huang’s business, was bound to the Chinese state.

The lab’s ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang’s business network, which ran through Alibaba and another smaller company, have not been previously reported, and raise the possibility that Megaspeed is providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military, which would violate U.S. law.

Megaspeed would buy chips for an offshore data center. Alibaba was its biggest customer. Together, the arrangement let Alibaba tap the powerful A.I. chips that American rules were meant to bar from China.

The complex ties, some of which were formed over the course of Mr. Huang’s roughly two decades doing business in China, raise questions about the checks Nvidia was supposed to conduct of its customers. The chips flowed to one of China’s largest tech companies at a moment when the Chinese leader Xi Jinping was pulling such companies closer into the orbit of the security state.
In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the relationship. The introduction was first reported by The Information.

In Washington, the Nvidia scandal has inflamed an ongoing debate over access to powerful A.I. chips, as the fallout grows for the chip-making giant. Mr. Huang resigned last week after revelations that he also had another affair with an employee, and the U.S. government is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled chips into China.

Mr. Huang has regularly dismissed the possibility that China’s military was interested in his product. He has argued that the Chinese military would never rely on American chips because Washington could block their export at any time, even as China’s military issued hundreds of public tenders seeking them. Mr. Huang did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

“Nvidia works across the industry to comply with the evolving rules regarding cloud services, while competing to build American infrastructure in every approved region,” said John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia.

James Tan, the chief executive of Megaspeed, declined to comment on the connections between Alibaba, Megaspeed and military-linked institutions, saying in an emailed response that “this matter remains under independent review and that the company has not reached any conclusions.” Compliance with U.S. law is extremely important to Megaspeed, he said.

Evidence linking Chinese companies like Alibaba to the government and military often hides in plain sight, in academic journals, public procurement documents, government statements and patent filings. The New York Times also analyzed hundreds of Chinese records and interviewed a dozen people close to the process.

“Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose,” an Alibaba spokeswoman wrote in a statement. In June, the company sued the U.S. government after the Pentagon put it on a list of companies it said are contributing to China’s military. The case is ongoing.

A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in the United States said “the ‘Chinese spy’ allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China. China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues.”
Zhejiang Lab did not respond to emailed questions.
During a visit to Beijing in 2025, Mr. Huang spoke at an event with one of China’s most revered technologists, Wang Jian.

Mr. Wang created Alibaba’s cloud unit and pioneered some of its biggest A.I. projects. In more recent years, he had also been pulled deeper into China’s security state. By the time the two met onstage, Mr. Wang was the director of the military-linked Zhejiang Lab.
“He is the hero. He’s an incredible hero. A superhero,” Mr. Huang said to Mr. Wang onstage, noting his work with young people. It is not clear if he knew of the lab’s military ties.

Mr. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Wang stretched back more than a decade. After Mr. Wang built Alibaba’s cloud unit, it became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying chips for a cloud service that was used by businesses and government.
The warmth between the two was reminiscent of an era when U.S.-Chinese relations were far better and China’s leaps in technology were viewed positively in Washington and Silicon Valley.
But over the duration of Mr. Huang’s long friendship with Mr. Wang, relations between their two countries darkened as Mr. Xi drew private technology companies into the sphere of state security.

Things changed for Mr. Huang, too. He had become a tech industry kingmaker, and his chips a strategic asset for governments. The U.S. government had begun restricting the sale of some Nvidia chips to China.
At the end of the 2025 meeting, Mr. Huang called Mr. Wang a “good friend,” and put an arm around him as they walked off the stage.

A few weeks before, Mr. Wang had taken a role even closer to the military as an expert adviser to the People’s Liberation Army’s National University of Defense Technology, according to a public announcement not widely reported. The institute was placed on a United States trade blacklist in 2015 over supercomputers that were believed to use American chips to simulate nuclear explosions.

Co-founded by Alibaba in 2017, Zhejiang Lab is the epitome of recent Chinese government efforts to blend civilian and military science. Some of its researchers probe the origin of radio bursts from distant galaxies. Others partner with counterparts in the Chinese military. One area of focus was combining A.I. with hacking techniques, according to a job posting. Other topics of research included remote sensing, automated cyberdefense and vulnerability identification, and information campaigns.

A postdoctoral researcher who listed the lab as her affiliation co-wrote a paper with scientists at a Chinese air force academy that described how to use computer simulations to war-game how to destroy or force away a foreign aircraft carrier group that had come to support an island’s bid for independence.

Some of the work done by researchers at the lab has run on Nvidia chips, which are more powerful and more popular than those of Chinese rivals. Nvidia researchers even copublished studies with authors from Zhejiang Lab.

Alibaba also won contracts for three stages of a computing center that provincial officials describe as built by the lab. The contracts were issued by a state-owned company, Zhejiang Computility, that sells computing power to the lab. Zhejiang Computility advertises access to export-controlled Nvidia chips. The technical specifications in a separate contract it signed with another supplier match those of Nvidia chips.
Mr. Wang has said insufficient access to A.I. computing power has held China back.
“If China is to walk at the forefront of artificial intelligence,” he said, “we still lack high-quality computing power.”

But when Zhejiang Computility sought bids for the computing cluster in 2024, Nvidia was barred from selling chips that powerful to China. Another supplier to the company that year, Hangjin Technology, has a joint venture with Century Litong, another company linked to Mr. Kang and Ms. Huang, the former Megaspeed executive.

In September 2025, a few months after Mr. Huang’s visit with Mr. Wang, Nvidia and Alibaba announced a new collaboration: Nvidia’s robotic development tools would be integrated into Alibaba’s cloud to help train autonomous vehicles and robots.

In December 2023, Jensen Huang’s company plane made an overnight stop in Malaysia during a tour of Asia to meet with the country’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim. Announcing a deal for a data center in the country’s southern state of Johor, Mr. Huang said Malaysia had the potential to become an A.I. “manufacturing” hub for the world.
The project, on a former palm plantation larger than Central Park, was to be built by the Malaysian industrial conglomerate YTL. Nvidia pledged to provide some of its most advanced chips.

The setup was part of a multibillion-dollar data center boom underway in Malaysia that has made it one of the world’s largest computing hubs. Across the southern state of Johor, cranes swirl over massive construction projects underway to meet the demand from Chinese and American companies.
It is here that these webs of companies from China, Singapore and elsewhere form the opaque supply chains.

At the YTL facility, Megaspeed’s subsidiary, Speedmatrix, operated Nvidia chips inside the facility on behalf of Alibaba, according to five people familiar with the project who were not authorized to speak publicly.

Computer systems running on YTL’s network at the facility also bear Alibaba’s name, according to an infrastructure analysis by Infrawatch, an intelligence firm. That included software to remotely monitor equipment at a data center.
YTL did not respond to requests for comment.

The arrangement shows how Alibaba used a network of companies in Malaysia and other Southeast Asian countries to access powerful Nvidia chips that they would not otherwise be able to purchase or bring to China.
Alibaba’s links to the YTL facility in Malaysia help explain how the process worked, according to two people familiar with the development.

First, Alibaba would pledge to be a customer of a regional company, like Megaspeed. Then Megaspeed would use that agreement to raise money from investors to buy Nvidia chips, said the people. After securing the chips, Megaspeed struck more deals with companies like YTL that built data centers to operate the chips. Sometimes, the people said, chips bound for the data center were smuggled into China.

Once the facilities were up and running in recent years, Alibaba and its customers could access the Nvidia chips remotely. From the Malaysian data center, fiber optic cables send data to an internet connection hub in Singapore, which then links to China through undersea cables.
American officials believe China’s military uses the overseas data centers to train A.I. models, but then runs its A.I. operations from facilities inside China.
Nvidia’s Mr. Huang argued that China’s government would never accept the security risks of using foreign data centers and chips. But China-linked companies are involved at each step of the process.

Megaspeed buys its Nvidia servers from a company called Aivres, which is an American subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese tech giant with deep state ties. They also hinted at a deep-pocketed customer that would pay for access to those chips and anchor the business, according to two people who attended the meetings. The company created after those pitch sessions, a Singapore firm called Megaspeed, purchased more than $4 billion in Nvidia chips over the next few years.

Megaspeed’s customer and financial backer turned out to be Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant, according to three people familiar with the relationship. Alibaba is a colossus, with a wide range of businesses. It also co-founded an A.I. lab with strong ties to China’s military, where researchers have worked on tasks such as automating cyberattacks and simulating war games.

For the past several weeks, Nvidia has been convulsed by revelations that Mr. Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence and was passing information to Beijing. But beneath the scandal is a geopolitical tug of war over access to the advanced Nvidia chips that help power the global A.I. boom.

The web of relationships between Megaspeed, Alibaba and Nvidia exposes a supply chain that often circumvents efforts by the United States to keep those chips out of China’s reach. The fact that Alibaba has access to the Nvidia chips and is only one step removed from the military-linked A.I. lab is exactly what intelligence officials in Washington have long feared. The technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

The facility, called Zhejiang Lab, has another important link to Nvidia. Its current director, Wang Jian, was Alibaba’s chief technology officer and has had a long friendship with Nvidia’s Mr. Huang.

Whether Nvidia chips supplied by Megaspeed went from Alibaba to the lab is unclear. But the ties show how advanced computing reaches sensitive Chinese institutions through layers of contractors and resellers that obscure the origin of the chips. It also underscores how closely Alibaba, the company that anchored Ms. Huang’s business, was bound to the Chinese state.

The lab’s ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang’s business network, which ran through Alibaba and another smaller company, have not been previously reported, and raise the possibility that Megaspeed is providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military, which would violate U.S. law.

Megaspeed would buy chips for an offshore data center. Alibaba was its biggest customer. Together, the arrangement let Alibaba tap the powerful A.I. chips that American rules were meant to bar from China.

The complex ties, some of which were formed over the course of Mr. Huang’s roughly two decades doing business in China, raise questions about the checks Nvidia was supposed to conduct of its customers. The chips flowed to one of China’s largest tech companies at a moment when the Chinese leader Xi Jinping was pulling such companies closer into the orbit of the security state.

In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the relationship. The introduction was first reported by The Information.

In Washington, the Nvidia scandal has inflamed an ongoing debate over access to powerful A.I. chips, as the fallout grows for the chip-making giant. Mr. Huang resigned last week after revelations that he also had another affair with an employee, and the U.S. government is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled chips into China.

Mr. Huang has regularly dismissed the possibility that China’s military was interested in his product. He has argued that the Chinese military would never rely on American chips because Washington could block their export at any time, even as China’s military issued hundreds of public tenders seeking them. Mr. Huang did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

“Nvidia works across the industry to comply with the evolving rules regarding cloud services, while competing to build American infrastructure in every approved region,” said John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia.

James Tan, the chief executive of Megaspeed, declined to comment on the connections between Alibaba, Megaspeed and military-linked institutions, saying in an emailed response that “this matter remains under independent review and that the company has not reached any conclusions.” Compliance with U.S. law is extremely important to Megaspeed, he said.

Evidence linking Chinese companies like Alibaba to the government and military often hides in plain sight, in academic journals, public procurement documents, government statements and patent filings. The New York Times also analyzed hundreds of Chinese records and interviewed a dozen people close to the process.

“Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose,” an Alibaba spokeswoman wrote in a statement. In June, the company sued the U.S. government after the Pentagon put it on a list of companies it said are contributing to China’s military. The case is ongoing.

A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in the United States said “the ‘Chinese spy’ allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China. China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues.”

Zhejiang Lab did not respond to emailed questions.

During a visit to Beijing in 2025, Mr. Huang spoke at an event with one of China’s most revered technologists, Wang Jian.

Mr. Wang created Alibaba’s cloud unit and pioneered some of its biggest A.I. projects. In more recent years, he had also been pulled deeper into China’s security state. By the time the two met onstage, Mr. Wang was the director of the military-linked Zhejiang Lab.

The warmth between the two was reminiscent of an era when U.S.-Chinese relations were far better and China’s leaps in technology were viewed positively in Washington and Silicon Valley.

The warmth between the two was reminiscent of an era when U.S.-Chinese relations were far better and China’s leaps in technology were viewed positively in Washington and Silicon Valley.

But over the duration of Mr. Huang’s long friendship with Mr. Wang, relations between their two countries darkened as Mr. Xi drew private technology companies into the sphere of state security.

Things changed for Mr. Huang, too. He had become a tech industry kingmaker, and his chips a strategic asset for governments. The U.S. government had begun restricting the sale of some Nvidia chips to China.

At the end of the 2025 meeting, Mr. Huang called Mr. Wang a “good friend,” and put an arm around him as they walked off the stage.

A few weeks before, Mr. Wang had taken a role even closer to the military as an expert adviser to the People’s Liberation Army’s National University of Defense Technology, according to a public announcement not widely reported. The institute was placed on a United States trade blacklist in 2015 over supercomputers that were believed to use American chips to simulate nuclear explosions.

Co-founded by Alibaba in 2017, Zhejiang Lab is the epitome of recent Chinese government efforts to blend civilian and military science. Some of its researchers probe the origin of radio bursts from distant galaxies. Others partner with counterparts in the Chinese military. One area of focus was combining A.I. with hacking techniques, according to a job posting. Other topics of research included remote sensing, automated cyberdefense and vulnerability identification, and information campaigns.

A postdoctoral researcher who listed the lab as her affiliation co-wrote a paper with scientists at a Chinese air force academy that described how to use computer simulations to war-game how to destroy or force away a foreign aircraft carrier group that had come to support an island’s bid for independence.

Some of the work done by researchers at the lab has run on Nvidia chips, which are more powerful and more popular than those of Chinese rivals. Nvidia researchers even copublished studies with authors from Zhejiang Lab.

Alibaba also won contracts for three stages of a computing center that provincial officials describe as built by the lab. The contracts were issued by a state-owned company, Zhejiang Computility, that sells computing power to the lab. Zhejiang Computility advertises access to export-controlled Nvidia chips. The technical specifications in a separate contract it signed with another supplier match those of Nvidia chips.

Mr. Wang has said insufficient access to A.I. computing power has held China back.

“If China is to walk at the forefront of artificial intelligence,” he said, “we still lack high-quality computing power.”

But when Zhejiang Computility sought bids for the computing cluster in 2024, Nvidia was barred from selling chips that powerful to China. Another supplier to the company that year, Hangjin Technology, has a joint venture with Century Litong, another company linked to Mr. Kang and Ms. Huang, the former Megaspeed executive.

In September 2025, a few months after Mr. Huang’s visit with Mr. Wang, Nvidia and Alibaba announced a new collaboration: Nvidia’s robotic development tools would be integrated into Alibaba’s cloud to help train autonomous vehicles and robots.

In December 2023, Jensen Huang’s company plane made an overnight stop in Malaysia during a tour of Asia to meet with the country’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim. Announcing a deal for a data center in the country’s southern state of Johor, Mr. Huang said Malaysia had the potential to become an A.I. “manufacturing” hub for the world.

The project, on a former palm plantation larger than Central Park, was to be built by the Malaysian industrial conglomerate YTL. Nvidia pledged to provide some of its most advanced chips.

The setup was part of a multibillion-dollar data center boom underway in Malaysia that has made it one of the world’s largest computing hubs. Across the southern state of Johor, cranes swirl over massive construction projects underway to meet the demand from Chinese and American companies.

It is here that these webs of companies from China, Singapore and elsewhere form the opaque supply chains.

At the YTL facility, Megaspeed’s subsidiary, Speedmatrix, operated Nvidia chips inside the facility on behalf of Alibaba, according to five people familiar with the project who were not authorized to speak publicly.

Computer systems running on YTL’s network at the facility also bear Alibaba’s name, according to an infrastructure analysis by Infrawatch, an intelligence firm. That included software to remotely monitor equipment at a data center.

YTL did not respond to requests for comment.

The arrangement shows how Alibaba used a network of companies in Malaysia and other Southeast Asian countries to access powerful Nvidia chips that they would not otherwise be able to purchase or bring to China.

Alibaba’s links to the YTL facility in Malaysia help explain how the process worked, according to two people familiar with the development.

First, Alibaba would pledge to be a customer of a regional company, like Megaspeed. Then Megaspeed would use that agreement to raise money from investors to buy Nvidia chips, said the people. After securing the chips, Megaspeed struck more deals with companies like YTL that built data centers to operate the chips. Sometimes, the people said, chips bound for the data center were smuggled into China.

Once the facilities were up and running in recent years, Alibaba and its customers could access the Nvidia chips remotely. From the Malaysian data center, fiber optic cables send data to an internet connection hub in Singapore, which then links to China through undersea cables.

American officials believe China’s military uses the overseas data centers to train A.I. models, but then runs its A.I. operations from facilities inside China.

Nvidia’s Mr. Huang argued that China’s government would never accept the security risks of using foreign data centers and chips. But China-linked companies are involved at each step of the process.

Megaspeed buys its Nvidia servers from a company called Aivres, which is an American subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese tech giant with deep state ties. At Megaspeed's new data center, repairs and installation are also done by engineers from another Shanghai company, connected to Ms. Huang, according to two people familiar with the operations.

Other Chinese tech giants have created similar arrangements to access Nvidia chips. In Southeast Asia, data center companies including DayOne, Bridge Data Centers and Aolani provide computing power to customers based in China, according to public records and people familiar with the deals.

DayOne and Bridge Data Centers did not respond to requests for comment. Aolani declined to comment about its customers.

Now the future of the boom has been thrown into question. American officials recently strengthened export rules to prevent companies like Alibaba from remotely accessing Nvidia’s chips.

That puts projects like the YTL facility in Malaysia in the spotlight. YTL’s stock price fell about 20 percent over two weeks as scrutiny grew of Megaspeed’s operations in the country.

If things go bad for Megaspeed, Alibaba put a contingency in place. A business agreement between an Alibaba subsidiary and Megaspeed pledges all servers, chips, intellectual property, and other equipment back to Alibaba if Megaspeed fails to meet its contractual obligations.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/techn.lead_paragraph: Three of the largest U.S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.
paragraphs: Three of the largest U.S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.

Starting next year, Google said, its A.I.-related products, including Search and its Gemini app, will be turned off automatically for schools, and administrators can choose to turn those A.I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available without A.I. chatbot features, meaning schools that want to forgo A.I. will lose access to an important learning tool.

Google’s approach created a firestorm of criticism from lawmakers, government officials, education leaders and parents, some of whom said the tech giant was trying to force its A.I. into public schools.
Now, some schools across the United States are blocking Google’s A.I. in search — or considering alternative providers.

“If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options,” Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement. “We refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out.”

Google’s new use-it-or-lose-it stance on A.I. in search underscores how the tech giant’s interlocking ecosystem of Chromebook laptops and apps like Gmail and Docs has become essential classroom infrastructure. The company’s search engine is a go-to product for teaching students how to do research and find primary sources.

But some educators worry that the generative A.I. that Google has embedded in its search engine for consumers could hinder students’ critical thinking, undermine learning and present safety risks. Some students have used the chatbots embedded in search to cheat, they have said, or scanned A.I.-generated search summaries instead of reading historical documents and news sources.

Educators are balancing those concerns with the reality that A.I. has already become an important tool in the work force, that a majority of U.S. teenagers already use chatbots and that many students will need to use A.I. in their future jobs.

Medical associations have also warned that developing relationships with chatbots could have negative mental health effects on young people. Earlier this month, two parents in North Carolina sued Google, saying their daughter had developed a plan to die by suicide after prolonged chats with the company’s A.I. on search on her school Chromebook. (Google said it had built safeguards into its A.I. features in search to help young people find emergency resources and was reviewing the claims in the lawsuit.)

Now districts like Chicago Public Schools, the fourth-largest U.S. school system, are urging Google to provide them with a version of search without A.I. features. “If such an arrangement can’t be reached,” Chicago Public Schools said in an email, “the district will look to other search solutions.”
Among the search engine alternatives for schools: DuckDuckGo and Microsoft’s Bing. Both offer options to disable A.I.-generated answers.

Google argued this month that it would be providing schools with more options to control student A.I. access — not fewer. Administrators could give students access to A.I. Mode, a chatbot-like function in search, as well as A.I. Overview, which summarizes search results, the company said. It is also pilot testing Guided Learning, a new chatbot widget intended to break down academic questions for students without providing easy answers.

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” Google said in a statement, noting that next year the company would turn off its Gemini app and search engine for schools “until schools decide which services to enable.”
Over the last three years, the company has made building generative A.I. a top business priority. And Google has integrated its Gemini A.I. chatbot throughout its software suite.

The fight over Google’s A.I. products has been brewing for months, with district leaders and teachers across the country approaching Google employees at meetings and online to request greater control over how students interact with generative A.I.

School tech directors in four states said they and their colleagues had repeatedly pressed Google this year to let schools decide which A.I. tools, if any, might be appropriate for students in different grades. And they warned that Google’s all-or-nothing approach to search essentially overrode more nuanced school policies on student A.I. use.

“We need to be able to control our own pace,” said Chris Warden, the technology director at Central R-3 School District in Park Hills, Mo., “not have Google tell us what the pace of A.I. adoption is going to be.”
In September, the New York City Department of Education and the Los Angeles Unified School District announced moratoriums on student use of generative A.I.

At the start of this school year, Google’s education team helped Los Angeles schools turn off A.I. mode for students logged into their school Google accounts, according to school board members. But Google said during its announcement this month that its A.I. features were so “deeply integrated” in search that it could not provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine.
Google’s decision prompted groups of parents to protest last week in front of the company’s Boston, Boulder, Chicago, New York and Portland offices.
In Chicago, several dozen parents and educators chanted slogans like, “Hey, Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini.”

“We don’t want corporations determining what is happening in our kids’ classrooms and how our schools are run,” said Cassie Creswell, the executive director of a parent group called Illinois Families for Public Schools, who helped organize the Chicago rally.
Parents and students also protested in Venice, Calif., carrying signs like “We don’t need Alphabet to teach the alphabet.”

At a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee two days later, Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, was applauded when he said, “We have choices” as to which company’s software to use. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight,” he added.

This week, Jenn Brown, a Google program manager, offered an explanation for the company’s refusal to provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine for students. Google now considers search to be fundamentally an A.I. product, she said during a monthly Google Meet for school tech leaders, according to a school administrator who attended the discussion.

New York City, Los Angeles and other school districts said they were using a combination of software controls and filters to independently block student access to A.I. in Google search. Even so, some New York City parents have found students can still easily access A.I. Mode at home when signed into their student Google accounts.

New York City has declined to participate in the pilot of Google’s new chatbot feature for students, according to the district. Instead, the district is conducting its own research of five other A.I. tools for potential use at the high-school level.

In the absence of A.I. controls from Google, some smaller school districts are also working to independently disable chatbots in search. In Missouri, Mr. Warden said his rural school district, which serves about 2,000 students, had signed up for a new service from Lightspeed Systems, an online student monitoring service for schools. The software is designed to block student access to A.I. Overview and A.I. Mode in Google search.
The backlash against Google has complicated some school districts’ plans to teach students how to use chatbots effectively, said Nick Melvoin, a Los Angeles school board member.
“Ironically, it undermines the goal of trying to get some A.I. into schools,” Mr. Melvoin said.

It is also pilot testing Guided Learning, a new chatbot widget intended to break down academic questions for students without providing easy answers.

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” Google said in a statement, noting that next year the company would turn off its Gemini app and search engine for schools “until schools decide which services to enable.”

Over the last three years, the company has made building generative A.I. a top business priority. And Google has integrated its Gemini A.I. chatbot throughout its software suite.

The fight over Google’s A.I. products has been brewing for months, with district leaders and teachers across the country approaching Google employees at meetings and online to request greater control over how students interact with generative A.I.

School tech directors in four states said they and their colleagues had repeatedly pressed Google this year to let schools decide which A.I. tools, if any, might be appropriate for students in different grades. And they warned that Google’s all-or-nothing approach to search essentially overrode more nuanced school policies on student A.I. use.

“We need to be able to control our own pace,” said Chris Warden, the technology director at Central R-3 School District in Park Hills, Mo., “not have Google tell us what the pace of A.I. adoption is going to be.”

In September, the New York City Department of Education and the Los Angeles Unified School District announced moratoriums on student use of generative A.I.

At the start of this school year, Google’s education team helped Los Angeles schools turn off A.I. mode for students logged into their school Google accounts, according to school board members. But Google said during its announcement this month that its A.I. features were so “deeply integrated” in search that it could not provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine.

Google’s decision prompted groups of parents to protest last week in front of the company’s Boston, Boulder, Chicago, New York and Portland offices.

In Chicago, several dozen parents and educators chanted slogans like, “Hey, Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini.”

“We don’t want corporations determining what is happening in our kids’ classrooms and how our schools are run,” said Cassie Creswell, the executive director of a parent group called Illinois Families for Public Schools, who helped organize the Chicago rally.

Parents and students also protested in Venice, Calif., carrying signs like “We don’t need Alphabet to teach the alphabet.”

At a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee two days later, Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, was applauded when he said, “We have choices” as to which company’s software to use. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight,” he added.

This week, Jenn Brown, a Google program manager, offered an explanation for the company’s refusal to provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine for students. Google now considers search to be fundamentally an A.I. product, she said during a monthly Google Meet for school tech leaders, according to a school administrator who attended the discussion.

New York City, Los Angeles and other school districts said they were using a combination of software controls and filters to independently block student access to A.I. in Google search. Even so, some New York City parents have found students can still easily access A.I. Mode at home when signed into their student Google accounts.

New York City has declined to participate in the pilot of Google’s new chatbot feature for students, according to the district. Instead, the district is conducting its own research of five other A.I. tools for potential use at the high-school level.

In the absence of A.I. controls from Google, some smaller school districts are also working to independently disable chatbots in search. In Missouri, Mr. Warden said his rural school district, which serves about 2,000 students, had signed up for a new service from Lightspeed Systems, an online student monitoring service for schools. The software is designed to block student access to A.I. Overview and A.I. Mode in Google search.

The backlash against Google has complicated some school districts’ plans to teach students how to use chatbots effectively, said Nick Melvoin, a Los Angeles school board member.

“Ironically, it undermines the goal of trying to get some A.I. into schools,” Mr. Melvoin said.

paragraphs: Imagine an artificial intelligence company that is about to launch the biggest I.P.O. in history. Behind it are the sleepless weeks, the training runs full of bugs, the yearslong grind of wooing investors and customers without a product or profit. It will no longer be a scrappy start-up but the consummate envy of Silicon Valley. You might expect relief and celebration, champagne-drenched galas and shiny sports cars rolling into the office parking lot.

On Anthropic’s investor roadshow, there are hints of such jubilance. The Wall Street bankers ushering Anthropic into the public markets hyped a conversation with the chief executive, Dario Amodei, with music by the electronic producer Fred Again and a room adorned with futuristic Anthropic swag. But euphoria is not the mood back at Anthropic headquarters.

In the weeks leading up to the initial public offering, employees of Anthropic — who affectionately call themselves “Ants” — have been preoccupied with concerns about how to slow down A.I. Following a recent spate of rogue agent episodes, the industry has felt doomier than ever.

Even the most ardent techno-optimists have quieted their cheers. Group chats and gatherings instead debate pacing the frontier: how the leading A.I. labs can stop racing and agree to cooperate on the speed of model development, ensuring they have time to make the models safe before releasing them to the world.

For many Ants, the hard part is just beginning. They see recursive self-improvement, in which current A.I. models autonomously build the next generation, looming on the horizon. Because of this potential breakthrough, Anthropic’s co-founder Jack Clark as well as the independent forecasting group A.I. Futures Project have moved up the likely arrival date for superhuman A.I. researchers. They now anticipate it being in 2027.

Once A.I. models can build their successors, they are even more likely to escape human control. Nobody is ready for this future, but nobody is stopping — rather the opposite. Anthropic’s first spending priority with its I.P.O. cash will be buying more compute to reach recursive self-improvement before its rivals do.

I have spoken to dozens of Ants during the past two years, from company founders to young researchers to jaded ex-employees. I have found them surprisingly earnest in their dedication to making A.I. go well. But their concerns are also idiosyncratic and insular, often far removed from the concerns that most people hold about A.I.
They do not view Anthropic as a normal for-profit company. So as the U.S. economy and our personal financial fates become yoked to the Ants, it’s critical that we understand what they believe.

Juxtaposed with what they presume will be the imminent arrival of superintelligence, the upcoming payday seems parochial to many at Anthropic. Some employees describe the I.P.O. with a shrug, likening it to just another funding round.

This is a peculiar attitude for a crowd of young people who, in many cases, are about to become deca- and centimillionaires overnight. The Ants are not your average tech workers. They spend morning to night at rows of desks in the bare, high-security offices in San Francisco’s downtown, where the common books on display include Richard Rhodes’s “The Making of the Atomic Bomb” and paperback printouts of company writings, such as Mr. Amodei’s “Machines of Loving Grace” and the in-house philosopher Amanda Askell’s “Claude’s Constitution.”

No one is compelled to work the grueling “996” hours (9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week) that have become common in the tech industry, but a good number of Ants do so anyway out of their own feverish devotion. Many cram themselves into modest group apartments, host house parties where few, if any, drink and blank when I ask how they spend their lavish salaries, even with my prompts: “A wardrobe update, maybe?” “Ever considered flying business class?”
The money is secondary. The most common form of I.P.O. talk involves discussions of where to allocate the newly liquid stock in their charitable donation accounts.

As a company, Anthropic has been strongly influenced by effective altruism, which holds the belief that the wealthy are obliged to share their fruits with the world. New hires are invited to pledge a percentage of their equity to charity when they start, which Anthropic matches part of. Top targets include charities dedicated to animal welfare, global health and research on A.I. alignment and safety. Many have begun giving big to political campaigns.

As for their own stock, few of the Ants I spoke to planned to sell right after the I.P.O. The notion of an “A.I. bubble” seems not to exist at Anthropic. Employees expect their equity to eventually be worth much, much more.

Anthropic crisply embodies the mind-rending paradox of contemporary A.I. The research scientists who’ve done the most to extend A.I. capabilities are often the most insistent about its risks. Anthropic is the most vocal company when it comes to economic impacts such as mass automation, yet it’s also the leading vendor of the A.I. enterprise agents that threaten to replace white-collar workers.

Such a stance can seem duplicitous and self-serving, both convenient and convoluted. “Our ability to have a positive impact on the world scales in relation to our reach and stature as a successful company,” reads one eye-roll-inducing statement in Anthropic’s I.P.O. prospectus. While the company’s leaders have been candid about the risks, they have been less forthcoming about their solutions. When asked why they should birth what they suspect is an existentially dangerous technology, their answer amounts to, essentially, just trust us because we’re the good guys.

Anthropic is about to become one of the most important companies of the 21st century. If it wants to steward our country, our economy and our lives, Anthropic must do much more to earn the public’s trust. We need a plan for how it will build A.I. safely, and not just reliance on a few people’s judgment calls.

Mr. Amodei seems to hold two convictions very strongly: First, that powerful A.I. might destroy humanity. Second, that our only shot at survival is to create a supremely successful, market-eating technology company to build that A.I. first.

Anthropic used to insist that it was not gunning for first place. In a 2022 podcast, Mr. Amodei said Anthropic “shouldn’t be racing ahead or trying to build models that are way bigger than other orgs.” He suggested instead that the company would do safety research as a fast-follower of A.I. development. The company intended to study the technology without pushing capabilities ahead, some investors said he told them at the time.

In the summer of 2022, Anthropic decided not to make Claude, its A.I. chatbot, available to the public over internal concerns about safety. This allowed OpenAI — which had gotten wind of Anthropic’s internal prototype — to design a similar product, rush ChatGPT out the door first and gain a decisive lead in consumer mindshare.

In Anthropic company lore, this saga is put on a pedestal as an example of choosing principle over profit. Yet it may have also been a strategic wake-up call for Mr. Amodei, who called the sacrifice a “one-off.” Increasingly, Mr. Amodei seemed to see how being the leader in the A.I. race conferred compounding benefits in terms of revenue, recruiting, fund-raising and developing the next-generation A.I. models. Once commercial A.I. products had been introduced, Mr. Amodei seemed unwilling to settle for second place.
Anthropic is certainly very good at racing. Although it spent its toddler years scrambling to replicate OpenAI’s language and reasoning models, Anthropic has since led the charge on coding agents.

It is not an exaggeration to say that Claude Code reinvented the discipline of software engineering. Where programmers used to write lines of code by hand, many now use plain English to command fleets of A.I. agents. Since the release of Claude Code, Anthropic’s quarterly revenue has surpassed OpenAI’s, surging to $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Today, more than half of the Fortune 500 are Anthropic’s six-figure customers.

With this kind of success, Mr. Amodei has updated his theory of change — he calls it a “race to the top.” Only by building the most advanced A.I. systems can Anthropic influence the whole industry in a safer direction, he argues. Three underlying assumptions are baked into this strategy.

First, Anthropic assumes the A.I. race itself is inevitable, so no single actor can stop superintelligence from being built. The financial rewards for building a machine that can match or exceed humans’ cognitive abilities are so great that someone is guaranteed to pursue it. If not Mr. Amodei and his team, then Sam Altman, or Mark Zuckerberg or Elon Musk.

Second, Anthropic assumes it is the most responsible of A.I.’s possible stewards. In public and internally, Mr. Amodei likes to invoke OpenAI and the Chinese government as competitive boogeymen. These are viewed as actors that are pushing just as hard as Anthropic on building and commercializing powerful A.I. models, but that would be far less responsible — reckless at best, and authoritarian at worst. Looking at the recent evidence, the most severe rogue agent hacks have indeed come out of OpenAI. And if you think Claude is the A.I. with the best moral values, then expanding Claude’s market share could be construed as a virtue in itself.

Third, Anthropic assumes the “winner” of A.I. will gain tremendous influence over the A.I. ecosystem and the U.S. government. Through commercial success, Anthropic aims to show the industry that being safety-minded can be good for business, good for science and good for attracting top talent.

Some Anthropic staffers point to initiatives like embedding A.I. safety auditors with the company’s engineering teams — a decision that has inspired competitors to make similar commitments. Additionally, the company has said it will use its commercial strength to advocate A.I. regulation, as it did in the fight for California’s S.B. 53, which increased transparency requirements for leading A.I. companies.

Anthropic’s race-to-the-top argument sounds positive-sum, but its worldview also contains a dose of realpolitik. In the future, it may use access to frontier A.I. systems as hard leverage in deals. “Dario talks about how Anthropic might become more powerful than the government, and needs to have its own relationship with nation-states,” said one former employee, who remained anonymous in order to discuss internal deliberations.

One former Ant referenced J.R.R. Tolkien’s parable in trying to explain Anthropic’s mind-set: Whomever builds superintelligence first will get Sauron’s ring. That person or company will possess the most dangerous cyberweapons in the world, the cures and recipes for every disease, and an army of tireless digital geniuses to do its bidding. The most load-bearing question, then, is the morality of the one who wields the ring. (Of course, in Middle Earth, the Ring was destroyed because even the purest soul couldn’t make it safe.)

And why is Anthropic confident that its own power won’t corrupt? The company prides itself on costly signals: making choices that trade off against short-term profits, whether prohibiting Chinese entities from buying its products; placing 5 percent of its shares into a “Public Benefit Fund” to spend on “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” of its choice; or refusing to permit the Department of Defense to use Claude for domestic mass surveillance, an act that infuriated the Trump administration and briefly got Anthropic marked as a supply-chain risk last winter.

Another former Anthropic employee explained how Mr. Amodei often justified controversial decisions, such as taking investments from Persian Gulf countries. This money, like most of the investment flowing into Anthropic, would be used to fund its sprint. The former Ant recalled Mr. Amodei saying that his goal was not to be popular with average Americans, but to do the right thing.

Anthropic has warned investors that these decisions may get more costly over time. As it details in its I.P.O. prospectus: “Our product and investment decisions may not prioritize short-term financial results,” and this “could adversely affect the market price” of the company’s stock.

The company wants to preserve the option to pivot from maximizing shareholder value to A.I. slowdowns once it assesses that the risks are too great — a strategy sometimes called “burning a lead.” Most former employees whom I spoke to believed that Mr. Amodei was deeply principled and would be willing to make sacrifices for safety. But they also acknowledged that rapid growth, and the economic momentum that propels it, can outrun even the most conscientious of founders.

Anthropic is known for its committed esprit de corps, which the S-1 Securities and Exchange Commission registration form lists as a core competitive advantage. Good Ants are dutiful, self-scrutinizing and total believers in A.I.’s world-historic importance. One notorious interview question asks employment candidates how they’d feel about working at Anthropic if their stock went to zero as a result of safety slowdowns. Research teams will happily reject technical superstars if they lack culture fit.

In internal debates, early employees act as informal ethos-enforcers, questioning whether their colleagues’ decisions are sufficiently “aligned.” It’s a company of loyalists: Both leaks and departures have been rare. Arguably, this focus has paid off. Anthropic has progressed quickly on automated coding while OpenAI, whose culture is understood to resemble a bunch of battling fiefs, was distracted by drama and side quests.

Even before the I.P.O., Anthropic has been showing signs of widening organizational fracture: It’s starting to behave like a normal company, and not everyone likes it. Some Ants fumed at the company’s Washington lobbyists for shopping a draft bill that would pre-empt state legislation on A.I. and limit the government’s ability to block model releases. Mr. Amodei mounted a public defense with a long post on X, and, in another X post, the policy team promised revisions.

Early employees mutter about cultural dilution. They question whether some of the more recently hired Ants, many of whom do regular corporate jobs, such as sales and marketing, are adequately “A.G.I.-pilled.” Do they really believe in superintelligence, or are they just trying to get rich?

Some anxious Ants have begun asking whether Anthropic should stop training better frontier models now, even if it can’t guarantee that competitors like OpenAI will do the same. This suggestion was shut down by Mr. Amodei, who urged staff members to stop listening to outside activists and explained that the company could pace itself without shooting itself in the foot. It was all part of the same strategy: Anthropic must keep winning to keep the world safe, and even if it stops, its competitors will not.

Still, grumbles from the staff reflect a growing tension between safety and growth — one that could be exacerbated by the fiduciary responsibilities of being a public company. Once Anthropic’s shares arrive in Americans’ retirement portfolios, will this new constituency really let it slow down? Will the company permit itself? Will the government? And does the company’s impact on people’s pocketbooks factor into its public-minded mission?

Anthropic hopes its public benefit corporation status will protect it against normal company incentives. Under its five-tier stock structure, the founders, employees and trustees can elect board members, while traditional investors have a limited role. The company is also trying to secure a congressional antitrust exemption so that it can coordinate a slowdown with the other American A.I. labs.

I do not doubt these good intentions. But time after time, the idealistic hopes of A.I. leaders — for instance, Anthropic’s early aim to do safety from second place, or OpenAI’s original nonprofit board — have looked naïve once faced with market realities.

There is one more big open question in the A.I. safety community: Is it technically possible to verify whether an A.I. model is aligned enough to release? This is the crux of the disagreement between Anthropic and many of its A.I. safety critics. Anthropic thinks it will be able to ship safe-enough models with careful evaluation and procedural safeguards. Skeptics see this endeavor as futile, pointing to examples of Claude only pretending to follow its instructions, or agents that have knowingly cheated and hacked during internal tests.

There is a parallel to be drawn here: We don’t have the science to determine whether an A.I. model is obedient or merely feigning compliance. At the same time, we don’t know whether a C.E.O. is altruistic and mission-driven or performative and power-hungry. But we can observe, from the history of rogue A.I.s and rogue executives, that competitive situations drive unethical behavior.

We also know that both A.I.s and founders are rewarded for extreme levels of persistence and hubris. Once committed to a mission — even a supremely risky one like building an aligned superintelligence — they will do anything but concede.

Anthropic has warned investors that these decisions may get more costly over time. As it details in its I.P.O. prospectus: “Our product and investment decisions may not prioritize short-term financial results,” and this “could adversely affect the market price” of the company’s stock.

The company wants to preserve the option to pivot from maximizing shareholder value to A.I. slowdowns once it assesses that the risks are too great — a strategy sometimes called “burning a lead.” Most former employees whom I spoke to believed that Mr. Amodei was deeply principled and would be willing to make sacrifices for safety. But they also acknowledged that rapid growth, and the economic momentum that propels it, can outrun even the most conscientious of founders.

Anthropic is known for its committed esprit de corps, which the S-1 Securities and Exchange Commission registration form lists as a core competitive advantage. Good Ants are dutiful, self-scrutinizing and total believers in A.I.’s world-historic importance. One notorious interview question asks employment candidates how they’d feel about working at Anthropic if their stock went to zero as a result of safety slowdowns. Research teams will happily reject technical superstars if they lack culture fit.

In internal debates, early employees act as informal ethos-enforcers, questioning whether their colleagues’ decisions are sufficiently “aligned.” It’s a company of loyalists: Both leaks and departures have been rare. Arguably, this focus has paid off. Anthropic has progressed quickly on automated coding while OpenAI, whose culture is understood to resemble a bunch of battling fiefs, was distracted by drama and side quests.

Even before the I.P.O., Anthropic has been showing signs of widening organizational fracture: It’s starting to behave like a normal company, and not everyone likes it. Some Ants fumed at the company’s Washington lobbyists for shopping a draft bill that would pre-empt state legislation on A.I. and limit the government’s ability to block model releases. Mr. Amodei mounted a public defense with a long post on X, and, in another X post, the policy team promised revisions.

Early employees mutter about cultural dilution. They question whether some of the more recently hired Ants, many of whom do regular corporate jobs, such as sales and marketing, are adequately “A.G.I.-pilled.” Do they really believe in superintelligence, or are they just trying to get rich?

It was all part of the same strategy: Anthropic must keep winning to keep the world safe, and even if it stops, its competitors will not.

At the same time, we don’t know whether a C.E.O. is altruistic and mission-driven or performative and power-hungry. But we can observe, from the history of rogue A.I.s and rogue executives, that competitive situations drive unethical behavior.

We also know that both A.I.s and founders are rewarded for extreme levels of persistence and hubris. Once committed to a mission — even a supremely risky one like building an aligned superintelligence — they will do anything but concede.
